name: Benito Juárez
info: Benito Juárez, a Zapotec lawyer born in Oaxaca in 1806, was president of Mexico from 1858 until his death in 1872, leading the Liberals through the Reform War and the Second French Intervention.

facts.born: 21 March 1806 in the village of San Pablo Guelatao, Oaxaca, New Spain, to Zapotec peasants, Brígida García and Marcelino Juárez
facts.died: July 1872, of a heart attack, aged 66; buried in the Panteón de San Fernando in Mexico City
facts.role: Judge in Oaxaca (1842–1846); governor of Oaxaca from 1847 for one term; Minister of Justice and Religion (1855); Chief Justice of the Supreme Court (1857); 26th president of Mexico from 1858 until his death in 1872
facts.known: the Juárez Law; the Liberal side in the Reform War; the Reform laws of 1859; resistance to the Second French Intervention and the fall of Maximilian's empire; being the first Indigenous president of Mexico; a long and disputed tenure in office

t: Born to Zapotec peasants, orphaned at three and speaking no Spanish until he was twelve, Juárez became a lawyer, governor of Oaxaca and in 1858 president of Mexico.
He led the Liberals to victory in the three-year Reform War and then led the Republic against the French invasion, until the Second Mexican Empire collapsed in 1867 and Maximilian was shot.
His long tenure, his emergency powers and his decision to run again in 1871 drew opposition from fellow Liberals, among them Porfirio Díaz, who rebelled against him.
dyk: In 1858 Juárez became the first sitting Mexican ruler to leave the national territory, travelling by sea from Manzanillo through Panama City, Havana and New Orleans to Veracruz, where he arrived on 4 May.
ev: Benito Juárez is born in San Pablo Guelatao, Oaxaca, to Zapotec peasants
He graduates in law from the Institute of Arts and Sciences in Oaxaca and is elected to the state legislature
He takes office as governor of Oaxaca
As Minister of Justice and Religion under Juan Álvarez he is named in the Juárez Law
Juárez succeeds to the presidency as Chief Justice when Comonfort leaves the country, and the Reform War begins
At Veracruz his government separates church and state and nationalises almost all of the Church's properties
Maximilian is shot at Querétaro on 19 June, and Juárez re-enters Mexico City on 15 July
Juárez dies of a heart attack in July, during Díaz's rebellion

sections.early:
Benito Pablo Juárez García was born on 21 March 1806 in the village of San Pablo Guelatao, Oaxaca, New Spain, a settlement of about two hundred inhabitants, with straw huts and a small church, at the edge of a mountain pond. His parents, Brígida García and Marcelino Juárez, were Zapotec peasants, whom he later described as "Indians from the primitive race of the country". He had two older sisters, Josefa and Rosa. He became an orphan at the age of 3, his grandparents died shortly after, and his uncle Bernardino Juárez raised him.

Juárez worked in the cornfields and as a shepherd until he was 12. Until then he was illiterate and spoke only his first language, Zapotec, specifically Ixtlan Zapotec. That year he moved to Oaxaca City, where his sister worked as a cook, and took a job as a domestic servant in the household of Antonio Maza. In 1818, while the Mexican War of Independence was ongoing, he entered the service of the lay Franciscan and bookbinder Antonio Salanueva, who sponsored him for the priesthood after he showed promise at primary school. He entered the seminary in spring 1821, a few months before independence, and studied theology for six years before deciding he was not interested in the priesthood.
sections.rise:
Juárez transferred in 1827 to the Institute of Arts and Sciences, founded by the Oaxacan state legislature the year before. He was appointed a teacher of physics in 1829, became a judicial secretary to the municipal council in 1831, took his law degree in 1832 and was admitted to the bar on 13 January 1834. From the start of his career he was a partisan of the Liberal Party. He took cases of Indigenous villagers; when the people of Loxicha hired him to denounce a priest they accused of abuses, he lost the case and was jailed with them, which he later wrote strengthened his goal of destroying "the pernicious power of the privileged classes". He sat in the Oaxaca legislature from 1832. When Santa Anna's coup of 1834 dissolved it, he protested and was briefly imprisoned. In 1842 the Liberal governor Antonio León appointed him a civil and revenue judge, a post he held until 1846. On 31 October 1843 he married Margarita Maza, some twenty years younger than himself, from a socially distinguished family of the city.

In 1846 he sat in the triumvirate that governed Oaxaca and was elected a deputy to the national congress. He became governor in November 1847, balanced the state's finances, built roads and bridges, promoted education and published a Civil and Penal Code. After the Conservative coup of 1852 restored Santa Anna, Juárez was confined at San Juan de Ulúa and exiled to Havana and then New Orleans, where he worked in a cigar factory. When the Plan of Ayutla rose against Santa Anna in 1855, he returned and became Minister of Justice and Religion.
sections.deeds:
The Juárez Law, promulgated under President Juan Álvarez, brought clerics and soldiers, until then tried only in their own courts, under the civil judiciary. It was written into the Constitution of 1857, which ended Roman Catholicism as the state religion. On the resignation of Ignacio Comonfort, who was drawn into a self-coup, Juárez, as Chief Justice, succeeded to the presidency in January 1858. The Reform War began with repeated Conservative victories. At Guadalajara in 1858 the garrison mutinied and imprisoned him, and its colonel ordered the prisoners shot before Guillermo Prieto's intervention made the soldiers hesitate.

From Veracruz, where his government settled, Juárez issued on 7 July 1859 an agenda that included the separation of church and state, a more independent judiciary and road and railroad building. The laws of 12 July nationalised almost all Church property, made marriage a civil contract, gave the registration of births and deaths to the state and dissolved the monasteries. The Liberals entered Mexico City on Christmas Day 1860, and Juárez won the 1861 election. When France, Britain and Spain intervened over his suspension of debt payments, he led the Republic through the French occupation, from San Luis Potosí to Saltillo, Monterrey, Chihuahua and El Paso del Norte. After the last French troops left in March 1867, Maximilian was tried and shot, and Juárez refused appeals for clemency, including appeals from European governments.
sections.opponents:
Juárez's opponents came from both parties. His government negotiated the McLane–Ocampo Treaty in 1859, which would have granted the United States perpetual extraterritorial rights across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec; the United States Senate rejected it. The Ley Lerdo, written into the 1857 Constitution, nationalised Church properties and also the communal properties of Indigenous communities, to be sold off. His own measures drew the charge of autocracy. In 1864 Manuel Doblado and Jesús González Ortega accused him of acting against the constitution, and Juárez defended himself by appealing to necessity. When his term expired on 30 November 1865, González Ortega claimed the presidency as Chief Justice; Juárez argued that the clause covered only an interim presidency to arrange elections, which were impossible, and prolonged his own term by decree, which the Liberals generally accepted.

After the war he showed no mercy to the more important collaborators, and Santiago Vidaurri was shot without a trial. A request to congress in January 1868 for more presidential power led opponents to say he was becoming autocratic. Juárez had been in power for over twelve years when he ran again in 1871; he did not win the majority the constitution required, and congress decided for him on 12 October. Porfirio Díaz's supporters alleged fraud and proclaimed the Plan de la Noria on 8 November 1871. Juárez called Díaz a "latter-day Santa Anna".
sections.last:
Juárez's wife Margarita died of cancer in January 1871, when he was planning his run for re-election. His health suffered in 1870 and began to fail again in 1872. Díaz's rebellion spread through the country, and the government of Sonora joined it in December 1871. As late as July 1872 the military situation remained serious, because the government's victories had not been decisive. Juárez used the rebellion to attack entrenched groups within several states, using government forces to neutralise rebellious elements in state militias.

Juárez died of a heart attack in July 1872, aged 66. He had been ill for two days, seemingly without alarming symptoms. A death mask was made and he was given a state funeral. He was buried in the Panteón de San Fernando in Mexico City, where other Mexican notables lie. After his death Díaz's reasons for rebellion, fraudulent elections and presidential coercion of states, no longer existed. Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, head of the Supreme Court, succeeded him, and amnestied Díaz in November 1872. Díaz rebelled against Lerdo in 1876.
sections.legacy:
Juárez came to be seen as "a preeminent symbol of Mexican nationalism and resistance to foreign intervention", and Mexicans considered his tenure a second struggle for independence. His policies advocated civil liberties, equality before the law, civilian sovereignty over the Church and the army and a stronger federal government. The Reform he led had major institutional consequences: the expropriation of Church lands, the subordination of the army to civilian control, the separation of church and state and the liquidation of peasant communal landholdings. One account holds that it replaced a semi-feudal social system with a more market-driven one, and that after his death the lack of institutional stability led to the centralised autocracy of Díaz, the Porfiriato of 1876 to 1911, which collapsed at the start of the Mexican Revolution.

Juárez himself wrote little about his Indigenous heritage. His vision was that Indigenous Mexicans would assimilate culturally and become full citizens equal before the law. One biographer observes that he has been the object of so much mythology that it is almost impossible to uncover the facts of his life. The city of Oaxaca added "de Juárez" to its name, Ciudad Juárez, formerly El Paso del Norte, bears his name, and his birthday, 21 March, is a national holiday. Two of his sayings are well remembered: "Among individuals, as among nations, respect for the rights of others is peace", and "The law has always been my shield and my sword".

summary: Benito Juárez (1806–1872), a Zapotec lawyer from Oaxaca, became president of Mexico in 1858. He led the Liberals through the Reform War and the Second French Intervention, and his long tenure and re-election in 1871 brought opposition from fellow Liberals, including Porfirio Díaz.
references: Patricia Galeana, Benito Juárez: El hombre y el símbolo (Crítica, 2022)
notes: Death date: the lede gives 16 July 1872, the personal life section says a fatal attack on 17 July, the Death section says 18 July (and an announcement on the morning of the 19th). The text gives only 'July 1872'. The Personal life section also gives 'a heart attack in March 1872, the day before his birthday' and another on 8 July, left out.

Margarita Maza: article says 'adoptive daughter of his sister's patron' and also that she came from the Maza family where he worked; 'some twenty years younger' used. The article gives no end year for the governorship (one term from November 1847).

Isthmus treaty: article says 'ultimately rejected by the United States Senate'; stated so. Reform laws: the article ascribes the 12 July 1859 laws to 'a series of anti-clerical laws'; wording kept close.

Reform War start: the lede says Juárez succeeded 'in the early weeks'; the body gives his release 11 January 1858. Dates for the Pennsylvania MOLLUS, Dominican and Peruvian honours, the media portrayals, the extramarital children and Freemasonry were left out for space or as not central.

The article gives both the Ley Lerdo's nationalisation and 'La Reforma del Norte' as names of the period; only the first is used. Where the article says the Constitution of 1857 'integrated' the Ley Juárez, 'written into' is used.
The 'second struggle for independence' and 'semi-feudal to market-driven' judgements are the article's attributed or unattributed summaries; the latter is given as 'one account holds'.
Roeder's 1947 biography is flagged by the article as lacking citations; not used. References left empty for the editor.
